balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF (GAAP) is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Non-GAAP FCF is ServiceNow's own headline metric and guidance target; it differs from GAAP FCF mainly by the timing of cash payroll taxes the company pays on vesting employee equity awards, which it treats as a financing-like, non-operating cash use. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: management's FY guidance and buyback capacity are framed around Non-GAAP FCF margin, not the GAAP number, so the gap between the two lines is itself a reported KPI, not a derived one.

What to watch:

  • Non-GAAP FCF margin trend versus management's own long-term target
  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below. Almost all of it is subscription revenue recognised ratably over the contract term, but a small, growing slice -- self-hosted deployments, which must be billed upfront under ASC 606 -- is recognised immediately. That upfront piece ($492m in FY2025, up from $253m in FY2022) adds noise to the quarter-to-quarter growth rate that RPO growth does not have.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

rpo.title: Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO)
rpo.content:
RPO is contracted subscription revenue not yet recognised -- signed, non-cancellable commitments that will show up in future quarters' revenue. Current RPO is the portion due within 12 months; its share of total RPO shows whether the book is skewing toward shorter- or longer-dated contracts.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: RPO growth is management's preferred forward indicator because subscription revenue lags bookings by a quarter or more -- a RPO deceleration shows up here before it shows up in reported revenue. Current RPO's share has held near 46-48% for several years, so a move away from that band is the signal to watch, not the level.

What to watch:

  • Total and current RPO growth decelerating faster than revenue growth (an early warning)
  • Current RPO % drifting up (shorter deals, less visibility) or down (longer deals, more visibility but slower revenue recognition)

customersByACV.title: Large-account concentration
customersByACV.content:
Customer counts split by annual contract value (ACV): accounts paying $1M+ and the larger $5M+ cohort.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the platform's land-and-expand model depends on existing customers buying more modules over time, so growth in the $5M+ cohort is the clearest sign that expansion, not just new-logo wins, is driving RPO. The $1M+ cohort stopped being disclosed after FY2024 once it grew too large to be a useful cut; $5M+ is now the more informative figure.

What to watch:

  • $5M+ customer count growing faster than total customer count (expansion within the base)
  • Net-new large accounts versus existing accounts crossing the threshold

marginSplit.title: Subscription vs professional services gross margin
marginSplit.content:
Subscription gross margin is the margin on the core recurring-revenue business; professional services gross margin is the margin on implementation and consulting work sold alongside it.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: professional services is run near breakeven (and often negative) by design -- it exists to get customers onto the platform quickly, not to generate profit -- so the blended company-level GrossMargin column understates how profitable the subscription business actually is on its own, and overstates how much drag services creates when its margin dips further negative.

What to watch:

  • Subscription margin trend in isolation (the business that matters for the valuation)
  • Professional services margin swinging more negative (often a sign of self-funded implementation deals or partner-channel shift)

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For ServiceNow, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
